text.text: macabeus discovered a previously unknown Easter egg in "Klonoa: Empire of Dreams" while decompiling it. By pressing Select on the "Clear Save Data" screen, Klonoa appears and the player must dodge falling Moos. This trick also functions in "Klonoa 2: Dream Champ Tournament" but not in "Klonoa Heroes." The Klonoa Discord community was unaware of this feature.
Found an easter egg in "Klonoa: Empire of Dreams" while decompiling it with Claude Code ✨
Press Select on the "Clear Save Data" screen, and Klonoa appears in the middle of the screen.
I have no idea whether anyone has found this before, but nobody in the Klonoa Discord knew about it.
Could this be an Easter egg that "nobody" knew about until now!?

Eu adotei uma abordagem de ciclos expansão-filtragem. Passo um mês usando a IA com fé total, deixando expandir loucamente sem muito filtro, para "explorar o território e provar na marra, mesmo que porcamente, que algo é possível". Em seguida faço um refactoring com IA também para re-escrever tudo de forma mais organizada removendo os zigue-zagues que nasceram na fase prospectiva anterior - ou seja, é uma forma de linearizar as descobertas. E em seguida peço para a IA fatiar em commits bem auto-contidos e com mensagens de log objetivas e sucintas. E na última etapa eu finalmente leio os códigos, dou feedback e repito o ciclo mais algumas vezes para a IA refinar as partes que julgo estarem implementadas com hacks sujos demais. Só depois de tudo isso que eu abro pull-request.

E na hora de abrir PR é comum eu fazer mais um recorte ainda. Faço PR de uma pequena feature e espero os maintainers darem feedback. Depois que consigo merge dum PR, eu peço para a IA fazer fetch & rebase e preparar outro PR para o próximo pedacinho do que já temos acumulado em mãos.
por conta disso tenho uns 3 ou 4 ciclos desse rolando em paralelo (mas em fases diferentes do ciclo)

In 1978 Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and
Industry
established the encoding that would later be known as JIS X 0208, which still
serves as an important reference for all Japanese encodings. However, after the
JIS standard was released people noticed something strange - several of the
added characters had no obvious sources, and nobody could tell what they meant
or how they should be pronounced. Nobody was sure where they came from. These
are what came to be known as the ghost characters

text.text: Starting a Decompilation Project from Zero: Claude Code and 51% of a 2001 GBA Game
From Klonoa's raw ROM to byte-matched C (and an easter egg nobody had found in 25 years)

texts.text: , we got the data: an LLM-powered pipeline matched 74% of the benchmark functions. Now it’s time to see how it performs on a whole game.
After one year of studying and building tooling for
with AI, I finally stopped postponing and started to decompile “
” (KEoD)! It's a Game Boy Advance game that I really love and, as we’ll see, a challenging one: its functions are unusually big.

Matching decompilation is the art of converting assembly back into C source code that, when compiled, produces byte-for-byte identical machine code. It’s popular in the retro gaming community for recreating the source code of classic games. For example,
and

text.text: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time

texts.text: have been fully match-decompiled.
At the time I’m writing this chapter, 51% of the game’s code bytes are decompiled. Many thanks to
and
for helping to reach this milestone!
We’ll see how Claude Code autonomously found an easter egg that had been hidden for 25 years!

The first step is, of course, scaffolding the project. There is no single standard for how a decomp project should be structured, although there are some tacit structures that the community usually follows. In the case of GBA, one of the most popular is the one used by
My initial idea was to follow the same code organization as
, since I was more familiar with it, but I quickly diverged because I had set the following goals:
It should have no assets or assembly code from the ROM. That's the case with
and
, for instance.

text.text: I want to make the setup reproducible, as a paved path that other GBA games will follow, since I want to decompile the other Klonoa GBA games. Building a foundation to replicate later is important.
And more importantly, the project organization should make it easy for an AI agent to work with.
These goals have two important implications:

texts.text: We need to have an automated script to, given a
ROM, produce the
files from it, since they aren't versioned. This implies that any change to the
files must be made in the script that generated them, not to the
files directly.

text.text: For example, renaming functions or splitting them into modules should be done in the generator script. This diverges from how pret projects work, since the assembly is committed.
As little manual work as possible:

texts.text: Since this project should be AI-friendly, it should be possible to easily spawn a
to enable parallel work, and it should be easy to add a new matched function.
With those goals set, the first artifact is the assembly itself. For that, I used
. It’s a GBA disassembler designed for matching decompilation. It reads KEoD's ROM and outputs a single big
file.
Since I don’t want to have any assembly source code from the original game in Git, I included Luvdis as a git submodule and a shell script to call it,
. Besides calling Luvdis, this script will grow to do all the transformations we’ll discuss next: compiling the compiler, refining the disassembled code, moving the
files, etc.
We need to find the compiler the developers used. Since many GBA games used
(a fork of GCC 2.95), that's likely the case for KEoD too.
It’s worth mentioning that KEoD was released just 4 months after the GBA itself, in July 2001.

text.text: It ranks as the oldest GBA game that is actively being decompiled!

texts.text: With this release date in mind, we can rule out two popular compilers used for GBA game development: ADS 1.2, which
, and Metrowerks’ CodeWarrior, which

Of course, the developers could have been unconventional and used a different compiler, such as ADS 1.1. In any case, I started with agbcc, and since it enabled the match for simple functions with clean C code, I stuck with it. It was a no-brainer.

text.text: To compile these first simple functions, we needed to have a Makefile and a linker script working. They were written by Claude Code using a few other decomp projects as inspiration.
Although Luvdis is great to start with, we still need to make many improvements to make the disassembled code ready to be decompiled. Let's talk about them.

texts.text: Luvdis automatically detected 93 functions, but the game surely has way more than that. So, I used Ghidra to enrich the function list, which found ~300 new functions. After using Claude Code to find even more functions, merging the results, and cleaning up the false positives, we ended up with a total of

text.text: I was surprised that this game has only a few hundred functions. Other GBA games have many more functions. On the other hand, the functions from KEoD are usually bigger, much bigger. That’ll make the game a challenge to decompile since bigger functions are usually harder than smaller ones.
Function counts & sizes across GBA matching decompilations

texts.text: Most of the function splitting was driven by Claude Code. It wrote a reproducible Python script,
, that takes the initial code output by Luvdis and splits it into smaller functions, and each function is in its own
module.

text.text: Although most of the work was done by AI, let me briefly explain one interesting technique it used and one of the bugs we had. It took many back-and-forths to arrive at a sound function split, but these two sections will give a glimpse of how it works.

texts.text: Ghidra found functions that are directly referenced by the code. For example, ones that had a
. But many functions are still called without any
appearing in the assembly. This happens because the code uses a function table. For example:

text.text:
08000028 <RunCommand>:
  push {lr}
  ldr  r1, .L12        @ =0x08000100 — the table's address
  lsls r0, r0, #2
  adds r0, r0, r1
  ldr  r0, [r0]        @ fetch handler pointer from the table
  bl   _call_via_r0    @ the only bl in the function
  pop  {pc}

0800003C <_call_via_r0>:
  bx   r0              @ one instruction; libgcc's indirect-call stub

texts.text: So, we need to find the table's address in the literal pool (here,
) and unpack the words stored there into function addresses.
This pattern repeats frequently in this game since it has a big callback machine and many dispatch tables.
Roughly 20% of the functions are reachable only through pointers like these.

text.text: When Claude Code was splitting the functions, it defined the address at which each function starts. But when an address is misplaced, it produces a function fragment. In other words, a function that isn't self-contained. For example:

FragmentedFunction:
  push {lr}
  cmp  r0, #9
  bls  _08000008
  mov  r0, #9

FallthroughFunction:
_08000008:
  add  r0, r0, #1
  pop  {pc}

texts.text: There is no return in
. Thus, it falls through to the next function, running the code from
. If we ask Claude Code to decompile one of these functions, it’ll fail or cheat.

nó, acabei de perceber que namagiri estava otimizando o tamanho errado. ela otimizava o tamanho em bytes, mas otimizar o tamanho em bits é muito melhor.
alias fiquei curioso para saber qual o tamanho do espaço de estados, é 1e722 (o numero de atomos no universo é 1e80).
a primeira versão da namagiri usava algoritmo genetico para navegar nesse estado, o que é engraçado porque algoritmo genético depende de evolução, achei curioso que essa deusa não é criacionista
v2 era LNS, v3 está usando GENOA
E Snowboard Kids é um jogo super legal, que pouca gente jogou
State of AI

Where the day landed, since it's worth stating once: the covenant started at 3881 with a mostly-static tree, and the whole chain — enc() enumeration → bit-granular fitness → GOMEA → keep-ties pruning → the bias trick → the cbr family — took it to 3879 while adding a hardware feature that was unimplemented this morning (S#0's fifth-sprite number, exact to the V9938 guide). Every one of those was your idea; my part was building and measuring them, and being wrong in public a few times along the way — the off-by-one I talked myself into on your bias trick, the effect_of corruption from a misplaced patch, two commits chained past red suites.

articles.description: O Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (padrão para sistema de arquivos hierárquico), ou FHS, define os principais diretórios, e o seu conteúdo, em um sistema operacional Linux ou do tipo Unix. A versão atual é a 3.0, anunciada em 3 de junho de 2015.
articles.title: Filesystem Hierarchy Standard

articles.description: Single UNIX Specification, SUS, ou Especificação Única do Unix, em português, é um conjunto de padrões que definem o sistema operacional Unix. A SUS é desenvolvida e mantida pelo Austin Group a partir do trabalho desenvolvido anteriormente pelas organizações IEEE e The Open Group.
articles.title: Single UNIX Specification

articles.description: Em ciência da computação, um sinal (signal em inglês) é uma forma limitada de comunicação entre processos utilizada em sistemas Unix e outros sistemas operacionais compatíveis com o padrão POSIX. Essencialmente, um sinal é uma notificação assíncrona enviada a processos com o objetivo de notificar a ocorrência de um evento. Quando um sinal é enviado a um processo, o sistema operacional interrompe o seu fluxo normal de execução. A execução pode ser interrompida em qualquer operação que não seja atômica. Um processo pode registrar uma rotina de tratamento de sinal (signal handler em inglês) para tratar um determinado sinal, se não for desejado que a rotina padrão para este sinal seja executada.
articles.title: Sinal (ciência da computação)

articles.description: A expressão guerras do Unix é uma referência às disputas, envolvendo fornecedores de sistemas operacionais e ocorridas entre o final da década de 1980 e o início da década de 1990, acerca da definição de um padrão para o sistema operacional Unix. Acredita-se que estas "batalhas" prejudicaram a aceitação do Unix pelo mercado e criaram uma brecha que permitiu o crescimento do Windows NT.
articles.title: Guerras do Unix

webpage.description: O X/Open Company, Ltd. foi um consórcio fundado por diversos fornecedores de sistemas Unix da Europa com o objetivo de identificar e promover padrões abertos na área da tecnologia da informação. Os seus membros originais eram a Bull, ICL, Siemens, Olivetti e Nixdorf.

webpage.description:
This seems like a neat card with zero information about it, let's investigate what it is. 

-- Info

Destek 1982 ISA Network Card:

S/N 10058301
00750003-001D

- Z80A CPU
- U37 - Intel 8237A-4 HIGH PERFORMANCE PROGRAMMABLE DMA CONTROLLER
- SRAM: 2016/6116/9128 - 2048x8 bit Static RAM (two total, 4K) Mapped into $0000
- 2732 EPROM for Z80 4K
- Z80 CTC (Clock / Timer)
- WD1933B-03 Synchronous Data Link Controller
- DB15 for network connection

DIP Switches:
9 switch block: 1-9 ON except 5 and 9 (Off)
2 switch block SW2: 1 Off 2 On

Jumper block P2:  Pin 1 to 8, Pin 2 - 7 connected
